title: After the threshing floor: who “went into the city”?
summary: The KJV says “she went into the city”, meaning Ruth. The Hebrew verb is masculine: “he went into the city”, meaning Boaz.
text: KJV Ruth 3:15: “he measured six measures of barley, and laid it on her: and she went into the city”. Hebrew (WLC): וַיָּ֤מָד שֵׁשׁ־שְׂעֹרִים֙ וַיָּ֣שֶׁת עָלֶ֔יהָ וַיָּבֹ֖א הָעִֽיר [and he measured six of barley and put it on her, and he went into the city]. Aleppo-based edition (HAC), consonants only: וימד שש שערים וישת עליה ויבא העיר. Where Ruth is the one who goes into the city, the same book uses the feminine form: 2:18 וַתָּבֹ֣וא הָעִ֔יר [and she went into the city], KJV “And she took it up, and went into the city”; and 3:16 וַתָּבֹוא֙ אֶל־חֲמֹותָ֔הּ [and she came to her mother in law], KJV “And when she came to her mother in law”. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 3:15: καὶ εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὴν πόλιν [and went into the city; the Greek verb does not mark he or she]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/8/3/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/8/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/HAC/8/3/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/RUT03.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew verb form at 3:15 is masculine, the same form as “he measured” and “he put” just before it, and differs from the feminine form the book uses for Ruth at 2:18 and 3:16. The KJV changes the subject from Boaz to Ruth.
scope: Either way both people reach the town: Ruth is with Naomi in 3:16 and Boaz is at the gate in 4:1, so no event in the story changes. The difference is only who the sentence is about. The Greek verb fits either subject and is not counted as a Greek difference. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text, with the consonants-only Aleppo-based edition as a second witness. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined, and the KJV translators’ source for their wording is not established here. title: Boaz to the kinsman: “if thou wilt not redeem” or “if he will not redeem”?
summary: The KJV has Boaz say to the kinsman “if thou wilt not redeem it”. The Hebrew verb is in the third person: “if he will not redeem”. The Septuagint agrees with the KJV.
text: KJV Ruth 4:4: “If thou wilt redeem it, redeem it: but if thou wilt not redeem it, then tell me”. Hebrew (WLC): אִם־תִּגְאַל֙ גְּאָ֔ל וְאִם־לֹ֨א יִגְאַ֜ל הַגִּ֣ידָה לִּ֗י [if thou wilt redeem, redeem; and if he will not redeem, tell me]. Aleppo-based edition (HAC), consonants only: אם תגאל גאל ואם לא יגאל הגידה לי. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): εἰ ἀγχιστεύεις, ἀγχίστευε· εἰ δὲ μὴ ἀγχιστεύεις, ἀνάγγειλόν μοι [if thou redeemest, redeem; but if thou dost not redeem, tell me]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/8/4/, https://bolls.life/get-text/HAC/8/4/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/RUT04.htm.
reasoning: In the Hebrew the first verb is “thou wilt redeem” and the second, four words later, is “he will redeem”: two different forms side by side. The KJV prints “thou” for both. The Greek also has “thou” both times, so the Greek is not a difference from the KJV here.
scope: The sense of the conversation is not in doubt: Boaz is asking the kinsman for his decision, and the kinsman answers “I will redeem it”. The record is about the wording only: the KJV’s second “thou” matches the Greek and not the Hebrew of the named editions. Whether the Hebrew “he” is a slip, or Boaz turning to the elders for a moment, is not settled by the verse. title: The kinsman’s duty: buy the field “of Ruth”, or acquire Ruth?
summary: In the KJV Boaz tells the kinsman he must buy the field from Ruth as well as from Naomi. In the Septuagint he must also acquire Ruth herself.
text: KJV Ruth 4:5: “What day thou buyest the field of the hand of Naomi, thou must buy it also of Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of the dead, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance”. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κτήσασθαί σε τὸν ἀγρὸν ἐκ χειρὸς Νωεμὶν καὶ παρὰ Ῥοὺθ τῆς Μωαβίτιδος γυναικὸς τοῦ τεθνηκότος, καὶ αὐτὴν κτήσασθαί σε δεῖ [in the day of thy acquiring the field from the hand of Naomi and from Ruth the Moabitess, wife of the dead man, thou must acquire her also]. Hebrew (WLC), printed with two readings of the verb: וּ֠מֵאֵת ר֣וּת הַמֹּואֲבִיָּ֤ה אֵֽשֶׁת־הַמֵּת֙ [קָנִיתִי כ] (קָנִ֔יתָה ק). KJV 4:10, Boaz afterwards: “Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance”. Fetched from https://ebible.org/grcbrent/RUT04.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/8/4/.
reasoning: In the KJV wording of 4:5 the thing bought is the field, and Ruth is a second seller. In the Greek the kinsman must acquire two things: the field and “her”. Only the Greek wording of 4:5 states the duty that Boaz then says he has carried out in 4:10.
scope: The KJV follows the Hebrew words “and from Ruth” with no separate “her”; this is a Greek difference, not a claim that the KJV mistranslates the Hebrew. The Hebrew edition prints two forms of the verb (written and read); that marking is quoted for completeness and nothing is built on it. In every version the kinsman declines in 4:6 and Boaz marries Ruth. title: Elimelech’s field: Naomi “selleth” it, or it “was given” to her?
summary: The KJV says Naomi “selleth” the parcel of land. The Septuagint says the land “has been given” to Naomi, with no word of selling in the verse.
text: KJV Ruth 4:3: “Naomi, that is come again out of the country of Moab, selleth a parcel of land, which was our brother Elimelech”. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): τὴν μερίδα τοῦ ἀγροῦ ἥ ἐστι τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ ἡμῶν τοῦ Ἐλιμέλεχ, ἣ δέδοται Νωεμὶν τῇ ἐπιστρεφούσῃ ἐξ ἀγροῦ Μωὰβ [the portion of the field which is our brother Elimelech’s, which has been given to Naomi who returns from the field of Moab]. Hebrew (WLC), which the KJV follows: מָכְרָ֣ה נָעֳמִ֔י [Naomi sold / sells]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/grcbrent/RUT04.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/8/4/.
reasoning: The two texts say different things about the same field in the same sentence: in the KJV Naomi is disposing of it; in the Greek she has received it.
scope: The Greek still has a purchase in the next verses (4:4 “buy it”, 4:5 “from the hand of Naomi”), so both versions end with the field changing hands; the difference is confined to what 4:3 says. title: Ruth’s first day: a short rest “in the house”, or no rest “in the field”?
summary: The KJV says Ruth worked from morning “until now” and “tarried a little in the house”. The Septuagint says she stood from morning “until evening” and did not rest even a little “in the field”.
text: KJV Ruth 2:7: “so she came, and hath continued even from the morning until now, that she tarried a little in the house”. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): καὶ ἦλθε καὶ ἔστη ἀπὸ πρωΐθεν καὶ ἕως ἑσπέρας, οὐ κατέπαυσεν ἐν τῷ ἀγρῷ μικρόν [and she came and stood from early morning and until evening; she has not rested in the field a little]. Hebrew (WLC), which the KJV follows: מֵאָ֤ז הַבֹּ֙קֶר֙ וְעַד־עַ֔תָּה זֶ֛ה שִׁבְתָּ֥הּ הַבַּ֖יִת מְעָֽט [from then, the morning, and until now; this her sitting the house a little]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/grcbrent/RUT02.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/8/2/.
reasoning: Three points differ: “now” against “evening”, a rest taken against no rest taken, and “the house” against “the field”.
scope: The KJV stays with the Hebrew words “now” and “the house”, so this is a Greek difference only. title: Boaz’s instruction as Ruth reports it: “my young men” or “my maidens”?
summary: Boaz tells Ruth to stay close to his “maidens” (2:8). Reporting this to Naomi, Ruth says “young men” in the KJV and Hebrew (2:21), but “maidens” in the Septuagint.
text: KJV Ruth 2:8, Boaz: “abide here fast by my maidens”; Hebrew (WLC) וְכֹ֥ה תִדְבָּקִ֖ין עִם־נַעֲרֹתָֽי [and so shalt thou keep close with my young women]. KJV 2:21, Ruth’s report: “And Ruth the Moabitess said, He said unto me also, Thou shalt keep fast by my young men, until they have ended all my harvest”; Hebrew (WLC) עִם־הַנְּעָרִ֤ים אֲשֶׁר־לִי֙ תִּדְבָּקִ֔ין [with the young men that are mine shalt thou keep close]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2:21: Καὶ εἶπε Ῥοὺθ πρὸς τὴν πενθερὰν αὐτῆς, καί γε ὅτι εἶπε πρὸς μέ, μετὰ τῶν κορασίων τῶν ἐμῶν προσκολλήθητι [and Ruth said to her mother in law, Yea, he also said to me, Keep close with my girls]; 2:8 ὧδε κολλήθητι μετὰ τῶν κορασίων μου [keep close here with my girls]. KJV 2:22, Naomi: “that thou go out with his maidens”; 2:23: “So she kept fast by the maidens of Boaz”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/8/2/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/RUT02.htm.
reasoning: In the Greek, Boaz’s words and Ruth’s report of them match: “my girls” both times. In the KJV and Hebrew the report says “young men” where Boaz said “maidens”, and Naomi answers with “maidens” again. The Greek also has “to her mother in law” where the KJV has “the Moabitess”.
scope: This is a Greek difference; the KJV follows the Hebrew at 2:21. Within the KJV it is a difference between a speech and a character’s report of it, not between two statements by the narrator: Boaz also mentions his young men in 2:9, and the Hebrew masculine plural can be used of a mixed group of workers, so Ruth’s report is not shown to be false. title: Orpah’s departure: stated in the Septuagint, left unsaid in the KJV
summary: In the KJV Orpah kisses Naomi and the verse moves on to Ruth. The Septuagint adds that Orpah “returned to her people”.
text: KJV Ruth 1:14: “and Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her”. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): καὶ κατεφίλησεν Ὀρφὰ τὴν πενθερὰν αὐτῆς, καὶ ἐπέστρεψεν εἰς τὸν λαὸν αὐτῆς· Ῥοὺθ δὲ ἠκολούθησεν αὐτῇ [and Orpah kissed her mother in law and returned to her people; but Ruth followed her]. Hebrew (WLC), which the KJV follows: וַתִּשַּׁ֤ק עָרְפָּה֙ לַחֲמֹותָ֔הּ וְר֖וּת דָּ֥בְקָה בָּֽהּ [and Orpah kissed her mother in law, and Ruth clung to her]. KJV 1:15, Naomi: “Behold, thy sister in law is gone back unto her people, and unto her gods”. Fetched from https://ebible.org/grcbrent/RUT01.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/8/1/.
reasoning: The Greek narrator states that Orpah went back; in the KJV and Hebrew the narrator does not, and the reader learns it only from Naomi’s words in the next verse.
scope: No fact of the story differs: the KJV says the same thing in 1:15. The Greek clause is extra wording, and whether it was added in Greek or lost in Hebrew is not shown. The Greek “followed” beside the KJV’s “clave” is not treated as a difference in meaning.
